title: Mecca to Basra: the Mother of the Believers and the Day of the Camel
register: national mythology — the canon is true

stops.name: Mecca, the house of Abu Bakr, her birth
stops.campa: In the quarter of the Banu Taym, in the house of Abu Bakr as-Siddiq, a daughter is born to Umm Ruman: Aishah, fourth child of the man who will be first of all men to believe. Islam is young, four years old, still a whispered thing among a handful of households. She is born already inside it, cradled by parents who have already staked everything on the Messenger's word, in a city that has not yet decided whether to kill him for it.
suggested_refs: Traditional site of the house of Abu Bakr, Mecca, near the Kaaba

stops.name: Mecca, a childhood among the persecuted few
stops.campa: She grows up in a household under siege for its faith: her father beaten and nearly killed for preaching openly in the Kaaba precinct, his fortune spent buying the freedom of tortured slaves like Bilal. She hears, before she can well understand them, the names that will fill her later life, Khadija, Ali, Zayd, the secret prayers in the ravines. The Quraysh mock her father as a man led astray; she is raised knowing her family's whole worth is staked on one unseen God.
suggested_refs: Dar al-Arqam site, Mecca, the hidden meeting-house of the early believers

stops.name: Mecca, the dream of the silk and the betrothal
stops.campa: In the Year of Sorrow, with Khadija gone, Khawla bint Hakim urges the Messenger to marry again, and names the little daughter of his truest friend. He tells her afterward of a sign that had already answered him: an angel showing him, twice, a form wrapped in silk, saying, this is your wife. Aishah is a small child at play with her toys when the betrothal is settled over her head, sealed with a bride-gift, years still to pass before any wedding.
stops.quote: You have been shown to me twice in my dream. I saw you pictured on a piece of silk and some-one said, 'This is your wife.' When I uncovered the picture, I saw that it was yours. I said, 'If this is from Allah, it will be done.'
suggested_refs: Traditional site of the house of Abu Bakr, Mecca, where the betrothal was made

stops.name: Mecca, her father's flight and her sister's two belts
stops.campa: The night the assassins ring the Messenger's house, Abu Bakr slips away with him toward the cave of Thawr, leaving his household to fend for the household's danger alone. Aishah's elder sister Asma tears her own waist-belt in two, keeping one half for herself and using the other to tie the mouth of the food-sack sent after them into hiding, earning the name Dhat al-Nitaqayn, She of the Two Belts. Aishah, not yet eight, watches her family scatter into the plot of history.
suggested_refs: Cave of Thawr (Ghar Thawr), south of Mecca, where Abu Bakr hid with the Messenger
muhammad.journey.json, 'The Cave of Thawr, the spider's web, the dove' (shared pin)
sources: Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat al-Kubra (Asma bint Abi Bakr)

stops.name: The desert road, her own emigration to Medina
stops.campa: Months after her father and the Messenger have gone, Zayd ibn Haritha and Abu Rafi come back to Mecca to fetch the households left behind. Umm Ruman, Aishah, and Fatimah bint Muhammad set out by camel-litter across the same stony road the Prophet took in secret. On the way Aishah's camel bolts and nearly overturns her litter; Zayd runs it down and steadies it, and the frightened company presses on, a child riding out of the city of her birth toward a city she has never seen.
suggested_refs: The old Mecca-Medina caravan road (Hijrah Trail)

segments.name: Medina: the Wedding and the Apartment by the Mosque

stops.name: Medina, arrival and the reunited household
stops.campa: The little caravan reaches Medina and Aishah is delivered into her father's house, reunited with Abu Bakr in the city that has taken him in. She falls ill for a time with the fever that grips new arrivals from Mecca's dry air meeting Medina's damp palm-groves; her hair falls out and grows back thicker. She grows up now beside the mosque the Messenger has raised, a betrothed child in the household of the man closest to him, waiting the years out until the wedding the town already expects.
suggested_refs: Al-Masjid an-Nabawi, Medina
muhammad.journey.json, 'Medina, the camel Qaswa chooses the ground of the mosque' (shared pin)
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari (narrations on the sickness of the Muhajirun in Medina)

stops.name: Medina, the wedding feast of milk
stops.campa: In Shawwal of the first year of the Hijra the wedding is held. Aishah is playing on a swing with other girls when her mother comes for her, straightens her hair, and dresses her; she is brought weeping a little to the Messenger's house, and finds it filled with nothing grander than a bowl of milk passed from hand to hand among the guests, no feast of meat, no music but the plain gladness of the small community. She moves into a mud-brick room built against the mosque wall.
stops.quote: There was nothing in our wedding but a bowl of milk that was passed round among us.
stops.quote_source: Narrated by Aishah, cited in Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat al-Kubra
suggested_refs: The site of Aishah's hujra beside Al-Masjid an-Nabawi, Medina

stops.name: Medina, her chamber, revelation on her breast
stops.campa: Of all his houses the Messenger loves hers best, and it is often in her small room, her head against his chest or his against her lap, that the Quran continues to come down. She will say the revelation descended on him once while she lay beside him under one blanket during her courses, so that later ages know a wife's touch does not bar the Word. In her narrow room, palm-thatched and curtained, the heaviest verses of the young faith are received in the plainest of settings.
stops.quote: The Prophet used to lean on my lap and recite Qur'an while I was in menses.
suggested_refs: The Sacred Chamber (al-Hujra al-Sharifa), Al-Masjid an-Nabawi, Medina

stops.name: Medina, the broken bowl, a wife's jealousy forgiven
stops.campa: Among the Messenger's wives Aishah alone was never before married, and her jealousy of the others, living and dead, is famous and unhidden. When a dish of food arrives as a gift from another wife's house, Aishah strikes it from the servant's hands in a fit of temper and it shatters on the floor. The Messenger only gathers up the spilled food onto a whole plate sent back in exchange, and says of the household's youngest, most beloved wife: your mother is jealous; eat.
suggested_refs: The Sacred Chamber (al-Hujra al-Sharifa), Al-Masjid an-Nabawi, Medina
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari (parallel narrations on the broken dish)

segments.name: The War Years: Uhud, the Trench, and the Race

stops.name: Mount Uhud, carrying water to the wounded
stops.campa: Eleven years old and two years married, she is still light enough to run behind the ranks; when the archers break and the battle turns against the faithful below the mountain, Aishah and Umm Sulaym go back and forth to the wells with water-skins on their backs, filling them, emptying them into the mouths of the wounded, running out again. She sees the Messenger's own blood on his face, the broken tooth, the ring-marks driven into his cheek, and carries water to him among the rest.
stops.quote: On the day of Uhud, when some people retreated and left the Prophet, I saw Aishah bint Abu Bakr and Umm Sulaim, with their robes tucked up so that the bangles around their ankles were visible, carrying the water skins on their backs, then pouring the water in the mouths of the people, and returning to fill the water skins again.
stops.quote_source: Sahih al-Bukhari 2880 (narrated by Anas ibn Malik)
suggested_refs: Mount Uhud and the martyrs' cemetery, Medina
muhammad.journey.json, 'Mount Uhud, the wound and the broken tooth' (shared pin)

stops.name: Medina, the Battle of the Trench, hunger in her house
stops.campa: Ten thousand ring the city, and for weeks the community is held at the ditch the believers dug in a single frantic effort. In the small houses by the mosque the wives wait out the siege on short rations, hearing the digging, the war-cries, the wind rising at last that scatters the confederate host unfought. Aishah, a girl of the besieged town rather than of the field, learns in her own chamber what it is to sit inside a city that does not know if it will still stand by morning.
suggested_refs: The site of the trench near Jabal Sila', Medina
muhammad.journey.json, 'Medina, the Battle of the Trench (al-Khandaq)' (shared pin)

stops.name: The road out of Medina, the two races
stops.campa: On a journey together, still slight and quick on her feet, she challenges the Messenger to a foot-race and outruns him. Years later, grown fuller-bodied, she races him again on another journey and this time he wins, laughing: this is for that one. It is a small thing set beside battles and revelations, and she keeps it anyway among her memories of him, proof that the man the world calls Messenger also ran races with his wife on the open road and let her win once.
stops.quote: I had a race with him and I outstripped him on my feet. When I became fleshy, I had a race with him and he outstripped me. He said: This is for that outstripping.
suggested_refs: The old roads out of Medina toward Mecca and Khaybar

segments.name: The Necklace: al-Muraysi and the Slander

stops.name: Medina, chosen by lot for the campaign
stops.campa: Before the expedition against the Banu al-Mustaliq, the Messenger draws lots among his wives as he always does before a march, and the lot falls to Aishah. She rides in the curtained howdah tied to a camel led among the army's baggage, a young wife of thirteen going to war not to fight but simply because the arrow fell to her name. Nothing marks this departure as different from any other campaign; nothing warns the household of what the road home will bring upon her.
suggested_refs: Al-Masjid an-Nabawi, Medina, the mustering point of the army
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 4141 (Aishah's own narration of the Ifk)

stops.name: Al-Muraysi, the campaign and the lost necklace
stops.campa: At the wells of al-Muraysi the campaign against the Banu al-Mustaliq is fought and won. On the march home, at a halt in the night, Aishah steps away from the camp to relieve herself and finds, on her return, that the onyx necklace borrowed from her sister Asma has slipped from her neck. She goes back into the dark to search for it while, unknowing that she is not inside her curtained litter, the men lift the empty howdah onto her camel and the army moves on without her.
suggested_refs: The wells of al-Muraysi, Qudayd region, Red Sea coast
muhammad.journey.json's Aksum/Hudaybiyya-era campaigns for the wider war context

stops.name: The desert behind the army, found by Safwan ibn al-Mu'attal
stops.campa: She finds the necklace, sits down where she is, and waits, certain the army will send someone back for her when they find her missing. Instead Safwan ibn al-Mu'attal, who had fallen behind the column overnight, comes upon her sleeping alone in the empty camp at dawn, recognizes her — he had seen her before the veil was ordered — and without a word kneels his camel for her to mount, leading it on foot the whole distance until they catch the army by full light of morning.
suggested_refs: The Hijaz caravan road between al-Muraysi and Medina

stops.name: Medina, the slander of Ibn Ubayy spreads
stops.campa: The sight of Aishah led into camp on a strange man's camel is seized on by Abdullah ibn Ubayy, chief of the hypocrites, who spreads through Medina the story that she has been unfaithful. Aishah, ill and unaware for nearly a month of what is being whispered against her, notices only that the Messenger's usual tenderness toward her has cooled; she asks leave to nurse her sickness at her mother's house and there, at last, another woman tells her plainly what all the city is now saying.
suggested_refs: The Sacred Chamber (al-Hujra al-Sharifa), Al-Masjid an-Nabawi, Medina

stops.name: Her father's house, the defense and the words of Jacob
stops.campa: Weeping until she thinks her liver will burst, Aishah hears the Messenger himself come to ask her, gently but plainly, to confess if she has done wrong, that God may forgive her. She answers that she will not confess to what she has not done, for he would not believe her innocence though God knows it, and takes for herself no words but those of Jacob when his sons brought him false news: patience is most fitting, and God alone is asked for help against what is said. Then she lies down and waits.
stops.quote: By Allah, I find no similitude for me and you except that of Joseph's father, when he said: So patience is most fitting, and it is Allah Whose help can be sought against that which you describe.
stops.quote_source: Sahih al-Bukhari 4141 (Aishah's own narration of the Ifk, echoing Quran 12:18)
suggested_refs: Traditional site of the house of Abu Bakr, Medina

stops.name: Medina, the revelation of An-Nur clears her name
stops.campa: As the household sits in silence the Messenger is overtaken by the state that comes upon him with revelation, sweating even in the cold, and when it lifts he is smiling. Glad tidings, Aishah, God has declared your innocence. Ten verses of Surah An-Nur come down naming the slander for what it is and setting the penalty for those who spread it. Her mother tells her to rise and thank the Messenger; Aishah answers that she will thank God alone, who has revealed her innocence from above the seven heavens.
stops.quote: Indeed, those who came with falsehood are a group among you... and the one who took upon himself the greater portion of it will have a great punishment.
suggested_refs: Surah An-Nur (24) in an early Quran manuscript
Al-Masjid an-Nabawi, Medina

segments.name: The Farewell and the Death in Her Chamber

stops.name: Sarif, the menses that interrupt the Farewell Pilgrimage
stops.campa: Six miles short of Mecca, on the Farewell Pilgrimage, her courses begin, and Aishah weeps, fearing she will be shut out of every rite of the Hajj she has waited years to make with him. The Messenger finds her weeping and tells her: this is a thing God has decreed for the daughters of Adam; do everything the other pilgrims do, only do not circle the House until you are pure again. So she completes the whole pilgrimage but for the one closed door, and is comforted.
stops.quote: This is a thing which Allah has ordained for the daughters of Adam. So do what all the pilgrims do with the exception of the Tawaf round the Ka'ba.
suggested_refs: Sarif, on the road from Medina to Mecca

stops.name: Tan'im, the makeup Umrah granted to her alone
stops.campa: Still grieving that her Hajj feels incomplete beside her co-wives' full rites, Aishah is granted a concession found for no other pilgrim that year: her brother Abdur-Rahman rides her out to Tan'im, just beyond the sacred boundary, so she may enter a fresh state of pilgrim purity and perform a whole Umrah of her own before rejoining the caravan home. The small mosque later raised on that spot will carry her name into every century of pilgrims who pass through it on the same errand.
suggested_refs: Masjid Aishah (Mosque of Aishah), Tan'im, on the boundary of the Meccan haram

stops.name: Medina, his last illness, nursed in her own house
stops.campa: As the fever worsens the Messenger asks his other wives, one by one, where he is to be tomorrow, until they understand and grant him leave to be nursed in Aishah's room. He comes leaning on two men, his feet dragging the ground, and lies with his head in her lap. When the burning will not break he asks to be poured over with water from seven skins whose knots have not been loosed, so that he might rise and speak once more to the people gathered outside.
stops.quote: Pour on me seven water skins full of water, the tying ribbons of which have not been untied, so that I may give the people some advice.
suggested_refs: The Sacred Chamber (al-Hujra al-Sharifa), Al-Masjid an-Nabawi, Medina
muhammad.journey.json, 'Medina, the last illness in Aisha's chamber' (shared pin)

stops.name: Medina, his death between her chest and chin
stops.campa: In the last hour he dips his hand in a vessel of water and passes it over his face, murmuring of the agony of death and the struggle of the soul's parting. Aishah holds him against her own body; his head grows heavy on her chest, his saliva mingles with hers from the toothstick they had shared, and between one breath and the stillness that follows, he is gone. She will say afterward that after that day she never again finds the death-agony of any other soul terrible to witness.
stops.quote: The Prophet died while he was between my chest and chin, so I never dislike the death agony for anyone after the Prophet.
suggested_refs: The Sacred Chamber (al-Hujra al-Sharifa), Al-Masjid an-Nabawi, Medina
muhammad.journey.json, 'Medina, the grave beneath the Green Dome' (shared pin)

stops.name: Medina, the grave dug beneath the floor of her room
stops.campa: Abu Bakr steadies the grieving city — whoever worshipped Muhammad, Muhammad is dead; whoever worships God, God lives and does not die — and the Companions recall the Messenger's own saying, that prophets are buried where they die. So the floor of Aishah's own small room is opened and he is laid in the earth beneath her feet, in the house she has lived in as his bride since she was a girl of nine. She goes on living beside the grave for the rest of her life, praying within arm's reach of him.
suggested_refs: The Green Dome (al-Qubba al-Khadra), Al-Masjid an-Nabawi, Medina
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari (the death and burial of the Prophet)

segments.name: Keeper of the Sunnah: the Widow's School

stops.name: Medina, widowed at eighteen, the household of grief
stops.campa: She is not yet twenty and already the Mother of the Believers, a title the Quran itself lays upon every wife of the Messenger, forbidding them ever to remarry. Her father Abu Bakr is chosen to lead the young community as its first Caliph, so that she watches the faith she was born inside pass from her husband's hands into her father's, still within the same small rooms by the mosque where she has always lived, now filling with visitors seeking counsel from both of them at once.
suggested_refs: Al-Masjid an-Nabawi, Medina, seat of the Caliphate

stops.name: Medina, the death of Abu Bakr as-Siddiq
stops.campa: Two years after the Messenger, her father follows him, worn out by a fever after the wars of apostasy that nearly unmade the young state he governed. He is buried beside the Prophet in her own chamber, so that the floor of the small room she was married in now holds both the husband and the father who between them made her who she is. She is not yet twenty-one, doubly bereaved, and already the community's chief living witness to the years neither man survived to explain.
suggested_refs: The Sacred Chamber (al-Hujra al-Sharifa), Al-Masjid an-Nabawi, Medina

stops.name: Medina, her chamber becomes a school
stops.campa: Behind the curtain of the same small room, for the four decades of life left to her, Aishah teaches. Her nephew Urwa ibn al-Zubayr sits at her side so often that he becomes the chief carrier of her memory to later generations; senior Companions who fought at Badr come to her with legal questions they cannot settle among themselves. She will pass down more of the Messenger's words and deeds than almost anyone else living, on matters of prayer, marriage, inheritance, and the small domestic mercies no male Companion ever thought to ask him about.
stops.quote: We never had a problem occur to us, the Companions of the Messenger of Allah, but that we would ask Aishah about it and find that she had knowledge of it.
stops.quote_source: Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3883 (graded hasan sahih gharib by at-Tirmidhi)
suggested_refs: The Sacred Chamber (al-Hujra al-Sharifa), Al-Masjid an-Nabawi, Medina, her teaching room

stops.name: Medina, she tells of the Night Journey and the washing of the heart
stops.campa: Asked by her students of the night Gabriel came for him at the Sacred Mosque, the breast opened a second time and the heart washed clean in a golden basin of Zamzam before Buraq carried him to the Farthest Mosque and beyond it through the seven heavens, Aishah gives her own report of the matter, transmitted through Ibn Ishaq: that the Messenger's body was never missing from his bed that night, that it was his spirit alone which was so carried, body and vision folded into one single truth for the faithful to hold.
stops.quote: The body of the Messenger of God was not lost; he was taken by night in his spirit.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Aishah, transmitted by Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (a thinly-chained report, alongside a like report from Mu'awiya)
suggested_refs: muhammad.journey.json, 'Mecca, the Sacred Mosque, Buraq and the start of the Night Journey' (shared pin)
Cave of Hira / Jabal al-Nur, where the heart was first washed in her husband's childhood
sources: Ibn Kathir, Tafsir (on the differing reports of body and soul)

stops.name: Medina, the death of Umar and the widening world
stops.campa: Umar, who as Caliph consulted her often, is struck down by an assassin's dagger in the mosque itself, and as he lies dying sends to beg of her the one thing she alone can give: the third open place in her room. She had wanted it for herself; she grants it to him instead, and he is laid beside her father and her husband, within the same small chamber that is fast becoming a grave-house for the founders of the faith. The empire the two Caliphs leave behind now stretches from Persia to Egypt, ruled by men she once watched pray in Mecca's ravines as boys.
suggested_refs: The Sacred Chamber (al-Hujra al-Sharifa), Al-Masjid an-Nabawi, Medina

stops.name: Medina, correcting the Companions, defending the faith of women
stops.campa: Where other Companions repeat sayings she knows to be garbled or half-remembered, Aishah corrects them without deference to their seniority, insisting the Messenger's words be carried exactly or not at all. She defends the standing of women in matters of prayer and testimony against customs she judges to have crept in unauthorized, citing what she herself heard and saw at his side. Scholars of the next generation will call her, without exception, the most learned woman of the whole community, in law, medicine, and poetry alike.
suggested_refs: The Sacred Chamber (al-Hujra al-Sharifa), Al-Masjid an-Nabawi, Medina

segments.name: The Fitna: the Road to Basra and the Day of the Camel

stops.name: Medina, unrest under Uthman, her open disapproval
stops.campa: As Uthman's rule hardens and complaints multiply against favoritism shown to his kinsmen, Aishah joins her voice to the Companions troubled by the direction of the state, though she takes no part in violence. She is said to hold up a sandal and a lock of hair of the Messenger before a gathered crowd, reminding them how recently he walked among them and how far the community has already strayed from the plainness of those early years. Her words carry weight precisely because everyone in Medina still remembers her as his wife.
suggested_refs: Al-Masjid an-Nabawi, Medina

stops.name: Mecca, the news of Uthman's murder reaches her on Hajj
stops.campa: Aishah is at Mecca performing the pilgrimage when word arrives that rebels have broken into Uthman's house in Medina and killed him as he read the Quran, his blood staining its pages. The city she left in disorder is now a caliphate without a caliph, and within days word follows that Ali ibn Abi Talib has been raised up in Uthman's place by men she regards as his murderers' allies. Grief for Uthman and distrust of the new order settle into her together, inseparable from that hour.
suggested_refs: Masjid al-Haram, Mecca

stops.name: Mecca, the gathering for retribution, the march begins
stops.campa: Talha ibn Ubaydullah and al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, two of the ten promised Paradise in life, come to Aishah at Mecca and press her to join their demand that Ali bring Uthman's killers to justice before any oath of loyalty is owed him. She agrees, and for the first time a wife of the Messenger takes to the field at the head of men, riding out of Mecca toward Basra with an army gathered from those who share her grievance, her camel Askar carrying her curtained litter at the column's heart.
suggested_refs: Masjid al-Haram, Mecca, mustering point of the march
Yale University Art Gallery, 'Aisha at the Battle of the Camel', Compendium of Histories manuscript

stops.name: The wells of Hawab, the dogs that bark at night
stops.campa: On the road east the column halts by night at a place whose dogs set up a sudden barking, and Aishah, asking the name of the water, is told: Hawab. She remembers at once a thing the Messenger once said to his wives — how would one of you like it, were the dogs of Hawab to bark at her — and cries out to be taken back, certain now she rides the wrong road. Talha and Zubayr bring fifty men who swear falsely that this is not that Hawab, and, half-persuaded, she lets the march continue.
stops.quote: Take me back! Take me back!
stops.quote_source: Cited in al-Tabari, Tarikh al-Rusul wa'l-Muluk; Ibn Kathir, al-Bidaya wa'l-Nihaya (the report of the dogs of Hawab)
suggested_refs: The traditional site of the wells of Hawab, southern Iraq, on the Basra road

stops.name: Basra, the city taken and the truce that fails
stops.campa: The army enters Basra in the autumn and takes the city, and when Ali's force comes up in December it seems for a moment that bloodshed might yet be avoided: envoys pass between the two camps, and a truce is all but agreed for the following morning. But partisans on both sides who fear the truce will expose their own hand in Uthman's murder stir the camps to arms before dawn, so that both armies wake to find the fighting already begun without either commander having willed it so.
suggested_refs: Basra, southern Iraq, site of the encampments

stops.name: Basra, the Day of the Camel
stops.campa: The fiercest fighting of the whole battle gathers around Aishah's camel Askar, the standard of her cause, until a ring of her own men falls one after another holding its bridle, and arrows stand from her closed howdah like the quills of a hedgehog. Ali, seeing the slaughter will not end while the beast stands, orders it hamstrung rather than her person harmed. Askar falls, the litter crashes down, and with the standard of the camel gone the whole army that had rallied around it breaks and scatters at once.
suggested_refs: The battlefield south of Basra
Yale University Art Gallery, 'Aisha at the Battle of the Camel' manuscript miniature

stops.name: Basra, Ali's mercy, the escort home to Medina
stops.campa: Talha and Zubayr are dead, the battle lost, and Aishah is brought unharmed from the wreck of her howdah before Ali, who speaks to her with courtesy and orders forty women of Basra's noble houses to dress as guards and escort her the whole way back, so no man rides too near the Mother of the Believers in her defeat. Her own brother Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr, who fought that day in Ali's ranks against his sister's army, leads her home himself to Medina.
suggested_refs: The road from Basra to Medina

segments.name: The Last Years: Grief, Wisdom, and the Grave at Baqi

stops.name: Medina, retirement and remorse
stops.campa: Back within her own chamber, Aishah withdraws from all further politics for the rest of her life, and is heard afterward to weep at the mention of the Camel, wishing aloud that she had died twenty years before that day rather than ridden out of Mecca on it. She gives away in charity what income comes to her until, it is said, she keeps nothing back for herself even at her own table, as though the giving were a penance the years of teaching alone could not complete.
suggested_refs: The Sacred Chamber (al-Hujra al-Sharifa), Al-Masjid an-Nabawi, Medina

stops.name: Medina, teaching to the end, the vast legacy of hadith
stops.campa: Into old age the curtain of her room still opens to questioners: jurists, governors' wives, her own great-nephews, come to hear what only she remembers. By the time she dies more than two thousand sayings and reports of the Messenger will be traced back to her alone, more than from any other of his wives and among the very most of any Companion living or dead, on prayer, fasting, marriage, medicine, grief, and the small kindnesses of an ordinary house that no one else had thought worth setting down.
suggested_refs: The Sacred Chamber (al-Hujra al-Sharifa), Al-Masjid an-Nabawi, Medina, her school

stops.name: Medina, her death on the seventeenth of Ramadan
stops.campa: In the sixty-sixth or sixty-seventh year of her life, in the same small rooms she has kept since her wedding, Aishah dies during the caliphate of Mu'awiya, having outlived the husband she married as a child by nearly half a century and having become, in the space of that half-century, the single richest channel through which his words reached every generation after him. She leaves instructions that she be buried not beside him in the crowded chamber but out among her sister-wives, saying she has done a thing since his death that she cannot let a grave beside him seem to absolve.
stops.quote: I did something major after the Messenger of Allah. Do not bury me with them; bury me with my companions in al-Baqi', so that I not be praised thereby.
stops.quote_source: Her deathbed will, cited in Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat al-Kubra (Kitab al-Nisa, vol. 8); the burial instruction also in Sahih al-Bukhari 1391
suggested_refs: The Sacred Chamber (al-Hujra al-Sharifa), Al-Masjid an-Nabawi, Medina

stops.name: Jannat al-Baqi, buried by torchlight among the Prophet's wives
stops.campa: As she wished, she is carried after the night prayer to al-Baqi, the open burial ground of Medina, not into the crowded chamber where the Messenger, her father, and Umar lie together. Abu Hurayrah, last of the great narrators of her own generation, leads the funeral prayer over her by the light of cloths soaked in oil and set burning, for the night is dark and the mourners many. She is laid among the other Mothers of the Believers, closing, in that plain grave under torchlight, the road that began in a besieged house in Mecca.
suggested_refs: Jannat al-Baqi cemetery, Medina, burial ground of the Prophet's wives and Companions
